# Every minimum-base-variance two-piece convex partition can have bad centroids

Consider the actual body

    C=[-1,2] x [0,1],
    S={-1,0,1,2} x [0,1],    mu(S)=4.

Among all exhaustive partitions into at most two positive-mass convex
subbodies with integer-base true centroids, EVERY partition minimizing the
mass-weighted squared base centroid has both of its centroids at normalized
mixed depth at most `9/40<1/4`. There are exactly two possible source
partitions at that minimum, up to labels and null boundaries.

Moreover the bad cap at each such centroid has ZERO source mass outside
its own piece. Thus a guaranteed positive outside-piece compensation cannot
repair this selector. This is not an OC counterexample, nor a failure of
the exact convex partition theorem.

## 1. Minimum variance forces exactly two prescribed class moments

The source has base first moment two and total mass four. Every possible
integer base centroid lies in {-1,0,1,2}. For every integer j,

    j^2>=j,

with equality exactly at j=0,1. Therefore every fractional or geometric
partition with masses m_i and integer centroids j_i has objective

    sum_i m_i j_i^2 >= sum_i m_i j_i=2.

The cap partitions constructed in Section 4 attain two, so this minimum
is feasible. Every positive class at any minimum has base zero or one.
The total moment equations then force mass two at each base. With at most
two positive pieces there are exactly two, which we label D_0,D_1, with

    mu(D_0)=mu(D_1)=2,
    integral_(D_0) z dmu=0,  integral_(D_1) z dmu=2.   (1)

We allow here even the superficially weaker geometric condition that the
closed convex pieces cover C and have null MIXED overlap. We do not assume
at the outset that their ambient interiors are disjoint.

## 2. The moment constraints exclude hidden ambient overlaps

The general assertion that null mixed overlap implies disjoint ambient
interiors is false: for example the pieces
`C intersect {z<=3/4}` and `C intersect {z>=1/4}` overlap in an open strip
containing no integer base. The following argument uses (1) essentially.

Suppose Q=D_0 intersect D_1 has nonempty ambient interior. Its projection
onto the base is a nontrivial compact interval [a,b]. At every base strictly
between a and b, its section has positive length. One direct proof is to
take an interior ball in Q and join it to a point of Q on the needed side
of the base; the resulting convex combinations supply an interval of
positive length in that section. Thus (a,b) contains no integer, since
otherwise mu(Q)>0. It follows that [a,b] is contained in one of the closed
unit gaps [k,k+1], k=-1,0,1.

Let s_z be the length assigned to D_1 in the unit fiber at z. The two
closed convex fiber traces cover [0,1] and intersect in a null set. If
`0<s_z<1`, both traces have positive length and meet at their common
endpoint. Hence that base belongs to the projection of Q. All split
fibers therefore lie among at most two adjacent bases k,k+1. Every other
s_z is zero or one.

The equations for D_1 are

    sum_z s_z=2,    sum_z z s_z=2.

After subtracting the other integral terms, both
`s_k+s_(k+1)` and `k s_k+(k+1)s_(k+1)` are integers. Their difference
forces s_(k+1) to be an integer, and then s_k is also an integer. This
also covers a single split fiber. Consequently every s_z is zero or one.
Exactly two bases are assigned fully to D_1, and their sum is two. Among
{-1,0,1,2}, the only such distinct pair is {0,2}. But a convex D_1 containing
both entire fibers at 0 and 2 contains their Minkowski midpoint, the entire
unit fiber at 1. That would give s_1=1, a contradiction.

Thus Q has empty ambient interior. Since both D_i are convex bodies,
their interiors are disjoint.

## 3. Reduction to one separating cap, including boundary cases

The two disjoint open convex interiors can be separated by a nonzero
linear functional. Taking closures gives a line L=0 with

    D_1 subset {L>=0},    D_0 subset {L<=0}.

Their union is C. Both pieces have nonempty ambient interior, so the line
crosses int C. Every point of C on the line can be approached inside C
from either side: join it to fixed interior points on the two respective
sides. Closedness therefore puts every such point in both pieces. Hence

    D_1=C intersect {L>=0},  D_0=C intersect {L<=0}.    (2)

The continuous x coefficient of L is nonzero. If it were zero, null mixed
overlap excludes a separating line at an integer base. A vertical cap of
mass two would therefore retain exactly the first two or the last two
integer fibers; their base first moments are -1 and 3, not the value two
required for D_1. Thus (2) is a nonvertical cap partition.

## 4. The only two source partitions and their four centroids

The upward-oriented feasible cap is

    H_+={x+z/5>=3/5}.

Its fiber lengths, in base order (-1,0,1,2), are

    (1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5).

They have mass two and base first moment two. Its continuous first moment
is `sum_z(m_z-m_z^2/2)=7/5`, so its centroid is `(1,7/10)`.

This source is the UNIQUE maximizer of the continuous first moment among
all dominated sources of those mass/base moments. Indeed, with
`L=x+z/5-3/5`, for every feasible density f,

    integral L(1_(H_+)-f) dmu>=0

pointwise; the mass/base terms cancel, leaving precisely the continuous
moment comparison. Equality forces f to equal the cap indicator almost
everywhere, because its nonvertical boundary has zero mixed measure.

Conversely ANY upward-oriented cap with those same source moments is a
continuous-moment maximizer by the identical sign argument using its own
affine margin. It must therefore be this unique source. Reflection in
`x=1/2` gives the unique downward-oriented source

    H_-={x-z/5<=2/5},

of centroid `(1,3/10)`. The complementary sources have base zero, mass two,
and continuous centroids 3/10 and 7/10, respectively. Thus EVERY minimizing
geometric partition produces one of the pairs

    {(1,7/10),(0,3/10)},
    {(1,3/10),(0,7/10)}.                              (3)

This uniqueness is for the actual source measures; it is already enough
for the centroid conclusion. In fact the four interior fiber thresholds
also determine the separating line uniquely.

## 5. Bad caps with no outside-piece contribution

At `(1,7/10)` use

    A_+={x+(3/10)z>=1}.

Its fiber lengths are `(0,0,3/10,3/5)`, so its mass is 9/10 and its
normalized depth witness is 9/40. On all of C, this cap lies inside H_+:
its lower x threshold exceeds that of H_+ by

    (1-3z/10)-(3/5-z/5)=2/5-z/10>=1/5.

Consequently

    mu(A_+ outside D_1)=0.

The affine symmetry `(z,x)->(1-z,1-x)` maps this partition pair to itself
with the labels exchanged. It maps A_+ to

    A_0={x+(3/10)z<=3/10},

which contains `(0,3/10)`, has the same mass 9/10, and lies entirely in
D_0 on C. Directly, its upper threshold is below the complementary H_+
threshold by `3/10+z/10>=1/5`. Reflection x->1-x treats the other partition
in (3), again with outside-piece mass exactly zero.

Thus all four possible centroids have an explicit cap below M/4, and
none of these witnesses receives any compensating mass from the other
piece. This rejects an automatic positive outside-piece charge for this
minimum-variance construction; it does not reject every possible global
relation involving other cap directions.

## 6. A nonminimal partition succeeds, and OC is unaffected

Partition C vertically at z=-1/2. The first piece retains only the fiber
at -1 and has centroid `(-1,1/2)`. The other retains bases 0,1,2 and has
centroid `(1,1/2)`. Their base-variance objective is `1+3=4`, strictly
above the minimum two.

The three-fiber subproduct `{0,1,2} x [0,1]` is centrally symmetric about
`(1,1/2)` and has mixed mass three. Every closed cap containing that point
therefore has original mass at least 3/2. The cap `x+z/2>=1` has exactly
that mass, so this point has depth 3/8>1/4 in the original source.

Hence the obstruction concerns EVERY geometric realization of the
minimum-base-variance partition, not every possible integer-centroid
partition. The original body satisfies the OC conclusion comfortably.

## 7. Every empty-target two-piece partition also fails

The obstruction is not specific to the quadratic objective. Suppose an
exhaustive convex partition into at most two positive integer-centroid
pieces has positive target-base set V in convex position with
`conv(V) intersect Z=V`. The original base mean is1/2, so V cannot be a
singleton. Two distinct integer points with an empty integer hull must
be adjacent; the only such pair whose convex hull contains1/2 is {0,1}.
Their masses are again forced to be two each. Sections2--5 then apply
unchanged, so all such partitions have only the bad centroids in (3).

More generally, minimizing any strictly convex base cost
`sum_i m_i phi(j_i)` over the finite fractional partition polytope forces
an empty target hull by the same proportional-row merging argument:
strict Jensen decreases the cost whenever an integer point is a
nontrivial convex combination of distinct positive targets. Thus changing
the strictly convex base cost cannot repair this entire empty-target
partition selector in the rectangle example. This still does not exclude
nonempty-target-hull partitions, such as the successful {-1,1} target
partition of Section6.
